title: S-M-Ch

lines: MAY WE SHARE IN MANY SMACHOT.
cards: "Mazel tov, may we share in many more smachot." It's a line heard at bar mitzvahs, weddings, a baby naming, a family party with too much food. Smachot is the plural of simcha.
In everyday Jewish English, a simcha isn't only a feeling. It's an event, with chairs and a caterer and an aunt who cries at the right moment. You don't usually have a simcha alone.
And the Torah's instructions about joy come with a guest list.

teach.b: S-M-Ch. Sin, mem, chet. Simcha: joy, gladness.
Sameach: glad. And the verb, to rejoice. First, joy as a command.
Deuteronomy, describing the harvest festival, says: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast." It's in the same voice as the other instructions. Some readers ask: how do you command a feeling?
One answer is that the Torah doesn't command the feeling. It commands the table, and the feeling tends to come and sit down. Second, the guest list.

teach.h: THE STRANGER, THE ORPHAN, THE WIDOW.
teach.b: The same verse keeps going: thy son, and thy daughter, the servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. The festival joy is meant to reach people who have no table of their own.

Maimonides, the medieval teacher, pressed the point hard. Someone who eats and drinks with family and locks the door against the poor and the bitter-hearted, he wrote, isn't rejoicing in a commandment.
That's the joy of the stomach. Third, worship.
A psalm sung in the morning prayers says: "Serve the LORD with gladness." The word for gladness is simcha. Fourth, the calendar.

teach.h: SIMCHAT TORAH: DANCING WITH THE SCROLL.
teach.b: At the end of the fall festivals comes Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah, when the reading ends and begins again, and the scrolls are carried around the synagogue with dancing.
Joy, in this root, is something you do, and something you do with people.

how: Jews call a family celebration a simcha; on the festivals the joy is traditionally widened to include guests, the poor and the lonely, and on Simchat Torah the scrolls are carried around the synagogue with singing and dancing.

o: the Hebrew root of joy and gladness

s: the festival joy in Deuteronomy is for your own family only
the verse lists the servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.
in Jewish English, a simcha can mean a party
a wedding, a bar mitzvah, a baby naming.
Maimonides called a locked-door feast the joy of the stomach
eating with family while shutting out the poor isn't rejoicing in a commandment, he wrote.

games.q: it's the harvest festival and your table is ready. who does Deuteronomy put at it?
o: you, your children, your servants, the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, the widow.
games.why: the verse keeps adding names until the people with no table of their own are at yours.

practice: Let one good thing from the last few days come back, a message that made you laugh, good news, a meal better than it needed to be, and feel it again.
Then picture one person who'd be glad to hear it, maybe someone a bit on their own lately, and hold their face in mind. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good thing.
